content: 1. Three authors evaluated the risk of bias in the included studies using the Cochrane Collaboration tool, ensuring a systematic and standardized approach to assessing study quality. 2. A total of eleven studies, published between 2010 and 2017, met the inclusion criteria for the analysis. These studies demonstrated that exercise interventions were more effective than control conditions in improving static balance in children with Down syndrome, as well as the combined static-dynamic balance (global balance score) in children and adolescents with Down syndrome. 3. However, the results regarding dynamic balance in children and static balance in adolescents with Down syndrome were inconclusive, indicating variability in the effectiveness of interventions across these specific domains. 4. The findings should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of studies included and the high risk of bias identified in these studies, which may limit the generalizability and reliability of the results. 5. The reviewed exercise interventions were successful in improving static balance in children with Down syndrome and combined static-dynamic balance in children and adolescents with Down syndrome, suggesting potential benefits of such interventions in this population. 6. Exclusion criteria for the studies included case studies, participants with a mean age below 18, studies not focused on balance interventions, non-interventional studies, studies without control groups, and studies involving infants. The outcomes addressed were static and dynamic balance or postural stability. 7. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to examine the effects of exercise, yoga, and physiotherapy on the physical, mental, and social quality of life (QoL) in individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS). The review included studies published between 1990 and 2017, with standard mean difference scores calculated for physical, mental, and social functioning domains. 8. Eighteen studies met the inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis. Aerobic exercise and physiotherapy were found to significantly improve physical, mental, and social functioning in MS patients, while yoga and combined exercise interventions did not show significant effects on any QoL domains. 9. The findings suggest that aerobic exercise and physiotherapy can enhance satisfaction with physical, mental, and social functioning in MS patients and may be considered as standard practice in MS management. 10. Quality of life (QoL) was categorized into three domains: physical health, mental health, and social health. The outcomes addressed in the studies included these QoL domains. 11. A systematic review was conducted to investigate the efficacy and safety of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) in individuals with MS. Seven studies were identified, including randomized controlled trials, a randomized crossover trial, and cohort studies. The studies predominantly involved participants with mild disability, with one study focusing on progressive MS. 12. Six studies used cycle ergometry, and one used arm ergometry to deliver HIIT. Adverse events were reported in one study, with four events attributed to the intervention, while the remaining studies reported no adverse events. 13. Improvements were observed in at least one outcome measure in six studies, with fitness being the most commonly measured domain. Fitness improved in five of the six studies assessing it. HIIT appears to be safe and effective in increasing fitness in individuals with MS and low levels of disability. 14. Further research is needed to explore the effectiveness of HIIT in individuals with progressive MS and those with higher levels of disability. 15. A systematic review was conducted to examine the relationship between physical activity and physical ability outcomes in individuals with MS. Twelve studies were included, evaluating endurance training, resistance training, and unconventional exercises such as tai chi, kickboxing, and vestibular rehabilitation. 16. Endurance training improved walking ability, while mindfulness exercises (tai chi and vestibular rehabilitation) and dynamic workouts (kickboxing) enhanced balance and coordination. Resistance training alone did not improve walking ability but increased lower limb muscular strength and endurance. 17. Combining resistance and endurance training resulted in improvements in mobility, balance, and coordination. Adverse outcomes were generally mild, ranging from muscle soreness to exacerbation of MS symptoms. 18. Physical activity was associated with measurable benefits in physical ability outcomes, but continuation of the activity is likely required to maintain these benefits. 19. A meta-analysis was conducted to determine the pooled effect of strength training on muscle strength and functional capacity in individuals with MS. Eleven randomized controlled trials were included, involving 426 participants. 20. Strength training consistently resulted in strength gains in individuals with MS. However, methodological inconsistencies and inadequate reporting limited the ability to comprehensively assess the impact of strength improvements on patient functioning, except for walking performance, which showed significant improvement. 21. Methodological steps and guidelines were provided to establish a common platform for future trials, ensuring consistency and reliability in research on strength training in MS. 22. A systematic review was conducted to synthesize evidence on the relationship between physical activity and cognitive performance in individuals with MS. Nineteen studies were analyzed, with nine reporting significant relationships between higher levels of physical activity or cardiorespiratory fitness and cognitive function. 23. Intervention studies reported mixed results on the effectiveness of physical activity in improving cognitive domains in individuals with MS. Correlational studies supported a linkage between physical activity and cognitive function, but confounding factors may have influenced the results. 24. Evidence from intervention studies supporting a positive effect of physical activity on cognition in MS remains equivocal, highlighting the need for further research. 25. A meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the effects of yoga on body structures and function, activity, and quality of life in individuals with stroke, MS, and children with cerebral palsy (CP). Yoga was found to be comparable to other exercise modalities as a treatment intervention. 26. Group yoga classes, typically conducted in social environments, may contribute to increased physical progress and improved quality of life, particularly benefiting individuals with CP. 27. More research on yoga, especially in children and adults with CP, is needed to develop effective and safe yoga programs with a wide range of benefits.
